Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 5–9:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾ ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that of which He has made you successors. For those who believe among you and spend, there is a great reward.﴾ ﴿And why do you not believe in Allah while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord and He has already taken your covenant, if you are believers?﴾ ﴿It is He who sends down upon His servant clear verses to bring you out from darkness into light. And indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to you.﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ is a report that encompasses all existing things. The word "al-umur" (matters) here is not the plural of the verbal noun; rather it refers to all existing things, because "al-amr" (matter), "al-shay'" (thing) and "al-wujud" (existence) are common terms applying to all existing things, both their accidents and their substances. The majority of readers recite "turja'u" with a dammah on the taa', while al-A'raj and Ibn Abi Ishaq recite "tarji'u" with a fathah on the taa'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾ — the verse is an admonition to reflect upon what the night and the day take from one another of length and shortness, which varies and differs according to the differences of regions and the four seasons. It is an ocean of the seas of reflection for whoever contemplates it. "Yuliju" means "enters" (yadkhulu). "Dhat al-sudur" (what is within the breasts) refers to the secrets and beliefs contained within them, which is the most hidden of things. This is like what they said: (p-220) "The wolf is envied for the one in its belly," and like what Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is only the one in the belly of the daughter of Kharija."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ — the verse is a command to the believers to remain steadfast in faith and to spend in the way of Allah. It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning the expedition of al-'Usra, which is the expedition of Tabuk, as al-Dahhak said. He said: the indication in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those among you who believe and spend﴾ refers to 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him. Its ruling remains, recommending these acts for the rest of time. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from that of which He has made you successors﴾ is an admonition to renounce worldliness and an alert that wealth only passes to a person from others and he leaves it to others, and he has of it only what is contained in the saying of the Messenger ﷺ: "The son of Adam says: 'My wealth, my wealth.' Do you have any wealth other than what you have eaten and used up, or worn and worn out, or given in charity and sent ahead?" It is narrated that a man passed by a Bedouin who had camels and said to him: "O Bedouin, to whom do these camels belong?" He said: "They belong to Allah with me." This is correct and right, if he is one whose words accompany his deeds.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And why do you not believe in Allah﴾ — the verse is a preparation for their invitation and an obligation, because they are the people of these elevated ranks. When this is established, there is no obstacle to faith. This is like when you wish to urge a man to generosity, so you say to him: "You, O so-and-so, are from a generous people, so it is fitting that you be honored." This applies in all matters: when you want an action from someone, you attribute to him the character of the people of that action and give him their rank. When it is established regarding these people that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invites them, and that they are among those whose covenant Allah has taken, then how (p-221) can they refrain from faith? The majority of readers recite "wa-qad akhadha mithaqakum" with the verb in the active form. Abu 'Amr recites "wa-qadukhidha" with the verb in the passive form. The one who takes [the covenant] in every reading is Allah, Exalted is He. This taking occurred when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, as has passed in other than this surah. Addressing with the passive form is more severe in its impact upon the one addressed, like the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112]. And like when you say to someone: "Do as you were told," it is more emphatic than your saying: "Do what I told you."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿if you are believers﴾ — al-Tabari said: the meaning is: if you are believers in some state of conditions, then now. This is a meaning not found in the wording of the verse and involves much implication. Rather, the meaning in my view is that the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord and He has already taken your covenant, if you are believers﴾ requires that there be implied after it: "then you are in noble ranks and high stations, if you are believers," meaning: if you persist in what you have begun with.

Some of the Seven readers recite "yunazzilu" with the intensive form, some recite "yanzilu" with the light form, and al-Hasan and 'Isa recite it in both ways. Al-A'mash recites "unzilu." The servant in His saying, Exalted is He: "upon His servant" is Muhammad ﷺ; "al-ayat" (the verses) are the verses of the Qur'an; "al-zulumat" (the darknesses) is disbelief; "al-nur" (the light) is faith. What is in the verse is a promise and a sure consolation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 10–11:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah, when to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought. And to each Allah has promised the best, and Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾ ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him, and for him is a noble reward?﴾

The meaning: "And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah while you are dying and leaving your wealth behind?" His saying, ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, takes the place of this statement. It contains an added reminder of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and a lesson, and from it follows the meaning we have estimated.

(p-222) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾, the verse. It is narrated that it was revealed because a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, spent large sums, so that people said: "These have greater reward than anyone who spent earlier." So the verse was revealed clarifying that spending before the conquest is greater in reward. This interpretation is based on the verse having been revealed after the conquest, though it has also been said that it was revealed before the conquest as an exhortation to spend. The first is more well-known. Al-Tha'labi related that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his expenditures. In the same sense is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him: "Leave my Companions alone, for if one of you spent the equivalent of Mount Uhud in gold, he would not reach the mudd of one of them nor half of it."

People differed regarding the conquest referred to in this verse. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and al-Sha'bi said: it is the Conquest of Hudaybiyya, and its being a conquest has been established earlier in Surat [al-Fath]. Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, traced it to the Prophet ﷺ: "The best of what lies between the two migrations is the Conquest of Hudaybiyya." Qatada, Mujahid, and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is the Conquest of Makkah, which ended the migration. This is the well-known view, concerning which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no migration after the conquest, but there is jihad and intention." And a man said to him after the Conquest of Makkah: "I pledge allegiance to you for migration." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed migration has gone with what it entailed." Its matter is severe, but I pledge allegiance to you for jihad." The ruling of jihad remains until the end of time. So whoever spends at a time of need for the way is greater in reward than whoever spends when the way is self-sufficient.

Most exegetes hold that His saying, "yastawi" (is equal), is attached to "man" (whoever), and the counterpart with which it is not equal is omitted, because His saying, ﴿from those who spent afterwards﴾, has explained and clarified it. It is also possible that the subject of "yastawi" is elided, its estimate being: "the spending of you is not equal," and this is supported by the mention of it having preceded in His saying, ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend﴾. Then His saying, "man anfaqa" (whoever spent), is the beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the following clause.

The majority of the Seven read: "wa-kullan wa'ada Allahu al-husna" (and to each Allah has promised the best). This is the preferred reading, because the promise of Allah is not hindered from making the preceding verb govern it in the accusative. Ibn 'Amir read: "wa-kullun wa'ada Allahu al-husna" (and each one, Allah has promised the best). As for Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, he took the verb as the predicate of an inchoative, with a returning pronoun in it, and its deletion is, in his view, ugly (p-224), occurring only in poetry and the like. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Umm al-Khiyar has become pretending against me a sin, all of which I did not commit."

He said: But they took the predicate as a description, like the saying of Jarir:

"... and nothing that I have protected is violated."

And as a relative clause, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra: 94]. Others besides Sibawayh held that "wa'ada" is in the position of a description, as if he said: "those, and each one whom Allah has promised the best." The proponent of this view fell into this strained meaning to flee from deleting the pronoun from the predicate of the inchoative. "Al-husna" means Paradise, as said by Mujahid and Qatada, and the promise includes what precedes Paradise of victory and spoils. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, is a statement containing both promise and warning.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan﴾, the verse. Some grammarians said: "man" is the inchoative, "dha" its predicate, and "alladhi" a description. Others among them said: "man" is the inchoative, "dha" is redundant with "alladhi," and "alladhi" is the predicate of the inchoative. Al-Hasan said: this verse was revealed concerning voluntary giving in all matters of religion. "Qard" (loan) and "salaf" and the like mean that a person gives something and awaits its recompense. "Al-taḍ'īf" (multiplication) from Allah, the Exalted, is in good deeds: Allah multiplies for whom He wills from ten up to seven hundred. It has been reported that the multiplication is increased beyond seven hundred. This has been mentioned in Surat [al-Baqara] with its interpretive possibilities.

Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-yudā'ifahu" with a nominative ending, as a coordination or as a resumptive new clause. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read: "fa-yudā'ifahu" with an accusative ending, by the fa' answering the interrogative. There is some difficulty in this. Abu 'Ali said: because the question did not concern the loan, but rather concerned the doer of the loan, and the fa' only puts into the accusative a verb linked to a verb that is the subject of the question. But this group construed it according to meaning, as if His saying, ﴿Who is it that would loan﴾, were equivalent to: "Would anyone loan Allah, so that He multiplies it for him?" Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 10–11:

The meaning: "And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah while you are dying and leaving your wealth behind?" His saying, ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, takes the place of this statement. It contains an added reminder of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and a lesson, and from it follows the meaning we have estimated.

He said: But they took the predicate as a description, like the saying of Jarir:

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan﴾, the verse. Some grammarians said: "man" is the inchoative, "dha" its predicate, and "alladhi" a description. It has been reported that the multiplication is increased beyond seven hundred. This has been mentioned in Surat [al-Baqara] with its interpretive possibilities.

Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-yudā'ifahu" with a nominative ending, as a coordination or as a resumptive new clause. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 12–14:

﴿On the Day you will see the believing men and the believing women, their light running before them and on their right: "Good news for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph."﴾ ﴿On the Day the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say to those who believed: "Wait for us, that we may borrow some of your light." It will be said: "Turn back behind you and seek light." So a wall will be set up between them, having a gate; its inside contains mercy, and its outside, facing them, contains punishment.﴾ ﴿They will call out to them: "Were we not with you?" They will say: "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, waited, doubted, and false hopes deceived you until the command of Allah came, and the Deceiver deceived you concerning Allah."﴾

The element governing "Day" (yawm) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for him is a noble reward﴾ [al-Hadid: 11]. The "seeing" in this verse is seeing with the eye. As for "light" (nur), al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: it is a metaphor, an expression for the guidance and truth which they hold, their guiding of people to the truth, and their truthfulness in deeds and words. It was also said: it is their following of right guidance, their belief in it, and their tracing of its traces, signs and lights. It was also said: it is a metaphor, an expression for the guidance and the pleasure of Allah in which they are. The majority of scholars said: rather, it is light in its literal sense. Reports on this from Ibn 'Abbas and others (p-226) contain the meaning that every believer who manifests faith is given light on the Day of Resurrection, while the light of every hypocrite is extinguished and the light of the believers remains. Among them is one whose light illuminates the distance between Makkah and San'a'; Qatadah traced this report to the Prophet ﷺ. Among them is one whose light is like a tall palm tree. Among them is one whose light illuminates only what is close to his feet; Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said this. Among them is one whose light sometimes wavers toward extinction and sometimes shines clearly, according to the ranks of their obedience and disobedience. Allah, exalted is He, specified "before their hands" because it is the place where a person most needs light.

People differed concerning His saying, exalted is He: "and on their right." Some interpreters (mu'awwilun) said: the meaning is "and from their right," so He specified the direction of the right for honour, and this took the place of saying "and in all their directions." Others among them said: the meaning is "and on their right are their books containing mercy." The majority of exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is that their light runs before them; He intends the spreading radiance from the people of light, and "on their right" is its origin, while the thing is kindled in it. The implication of this statement is that they carry the lights, and that their not carrying "them" is more honourable. Do you not see that the virtue of 'Abbad ibn Bishr and Usayd ibn Hudayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, was only through a light which they did not carry? This is in this world, so how will it be in the Hereafter? From this verse is derived the carrying of a candle by the one who frees a slave (al-mu'tiq lil-shama'a). People read "wa-bi-aymanihim" as the plural of yamin (right). Sahl ibn Sa'd and Abu Haywah read "wa-bi-imanihim" with a kasra on the alif, and it is coordinated with His saying "before their hands," as if He said: sufficient before them, and existing by means of their faith.

His saying, exalted is He: "Bushrakum" means: it will be said to them, "Your good news is gardens," i.e., entry into gardens. So the governing noun was omitted and the governed noun took its place. His saying, blessed and exalted is He: "abiding therein" to the end of the verse is addressed to Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read "dhalika al-fawz al-'azim" without "huwa."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say﴾. Some grammarians (nuhat) said: "Yawm" is a substitute (badal) for the first. Others among them said: its governing element is a hidden verb whose estimate is: "remember." He said: it appears to me that its governing element is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, and the meaning of triumph becomes more majestic, as if He, exalted is He, says: the believers triumph with mercy on the Day when such and such befalls the hypocrites, because a person's rising is most splendid and majestic on the day his enemy and opponent is humiliated. The hypocrites' saying of this statement that is related occurs when their lights are extinguished, as we mentioned before. Their saying "unzurūnā" means: wait for us. From it is the verse of al-Hutay'a:

"I have waited for you as the evening drought ends, for a long time my detention and my delay have lasted."

Hamzah alone, and Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, and al-A'mash read "anzirūnā" with a hamzah at the beginning, a kasra on the zay, on the pattern of "akrama." From it is the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"O Abu Hind, do not hasten against us, and grant us respite; we will inform you with certainty."

The meaning of their saying "akhkhirūnā" is: delay your walking for us until we catch up and borrow from your light. "Iqtabasa al-rajul wa-istaqbasa" means: the man took a brand (qabas) from the light of another.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It will be said: "Turn back behind you"﴾ may be from the saying of the believers, and it may be from the saying of the angels. His saying, exalted is He: "wara'akum" (behind you): al-Mahdawi and other exegetes related that it has no place in grammatical case (i'rab), and that it is as if he said: "Turn back, turn back," and that it is like the saying of Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali to the questioner: "Behind you is wider for you." I do not know of any prohibition against its governing element being "irji'ū" (turn back). The saying to them, "Seek light," is in the sense of rebuke to them, i.e., you will not find it. Then He, mighty and majestic is He, informed that He will set up a barrier between them in this state, with a wall; the hypocrites will then struggle in darkness, and punishment from Allah, exalted is He, will seize them. It is related from Ibn Zayd that this wall is the "A'raf" mentioned in surah [al-A'raf], and al-Mahdawi related it. It was also said: it is another barrier besides that. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, Ka'b al-Ahbar, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, and Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the eastern wall of the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis. Ziyad ibn Abi Sawadah said: 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit stood upon the eastern wall of Bayt al-Maqdis, wept, and said: "From here the Prophet ﷺ informed us that he saw Jahannam."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In it is a gate called the Gate of Mercy; 'Ubadah and Ka'b named it in the interpretation of this verse. In the east of the aforementioned wall there is a valley called the Valley of Jahannam; 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, named it in the interpretation of this verse. This view about the wall is far-fetched, and Allah knows best. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the mercy is Paradise, and the punishment is Jahannam. The "sur" in the language is the enclosure of cities (p-229), and it is masculine. "Sur" is also the plural of "surah," which is a piece of a building, so that some of it is joined to another until the wall is completed; this is a collective noun that may be made masculine or feminine. This is the plural that Jarir meant in his saying:

"When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Madinah and the lofty mountains humbled themselves."

That is because Madinah never had a ... (the sense of the word here is that the walls humbled themselves), and also because describing all the buildings of Madinah as humbled is more eloquent. Whoever sees that he intended the sense of "sur" as enclosure (hijā) says: if that humbles, then other buildings are more deserving of humbling. So when "sur" in the verse may bear both meanings, it is not in the strength of the passing of winds, the chest of a spear, and other things that are purely masculine, which took the feminine from what is attached to them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Its inside contains mercy﴾: that is, the side of the believers. "Wa-zāhiruhu" (and its outside): that is, the side of the hypocrites. "Al-zahir" here means the manifest side, and from it is the phrase in books: "from the outside of the city of such-and-such."

His saying, exalted is He: "yunadūnahum" means: the hypocrites will call out to the believers: "Were we not with you in the world?" The believers will answer them: "Yes, you were with us, but you exposed yourselves to temptation, to love of the transient, and to fighting over it." Mujahid said: "You tempted yourselves with hypocrisy." "Tarabbastum" here means: with your faith, you delayed in it until you died. Qatadah said: its meaning is: you waited for us and for Muhammad ﷺ for the reversals of fortune, and you doubted the command of Allah, exalted is He. "Al-irtiyab" is doubting. "The false hopes which deceived them" are their saying: "Muhammad will perish this year; Quraysh will defeat him; the confederates will seize him," and other such hopes of theirs. Prolonged hope is a deception for everyone. "The command of Allah that came" is the conquest and the manifestation of Islam; it was also said: it is the death of the hypocrites and their meeting Him in this state which necessitates punishment. "Al-Ghurur" (the Deceiver) is Satan, by consensus among the interpreters. Samak ibn Harb read it with a damma on the ghayn, and Abu Haywah too. It is fitting for every believer to take this verse to heart regarding himself, and regarding his procrastination in repentance.

As for "light" (nur), al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: it is a metaphor, an expression for the guidance and truth which they hold, their guiding of people to the truth, and their truthfulness in deeds and words. It was also said: it is their following of right guidance, their belief in it, and their tracing of its traces, signs and lights. It was also said: it is a metaphor, an expression for the guidance and the pleasure of Allah in which they are. The majority of scholars said: rather, it is light in its literal sense. Reports on this from Ibn 'Abbas and others (p-226) contain the meaning that every believer who manifests faith is given light on the Day of Resurrection, while the light of every hypocrite is extinguished and the light of the believers remains. Among them is one whose light illuminates the distance between Makkah and San'a'; Qatadah traced this report to the Prophet ﷺ. Among them is one whose light is like a tall palm tree. Among them is one whose light illuminates only what is close to his feet; Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said this. Among them is one whose light sometimes wavers toward extinction and sometimes shines clearly, according to the ranks of their obedience and disobedience. Allah, exalted is He, specified "before their hands" because it is the place where a person most needs light.

People differed concerning His saying, exalted is He: "and on their right." Some interpreters (mu'awwilun) said: the meaning is "and from their right," so He specified the direction of the right for honour, and this took the place of saying "and in all their directions." Others among them said: the meaning is "and on their right are their books containing mercy." The majority of exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is that their light runs before them; He intends the spreading radiance from the people of light, and "on their right" is its origin, while the thing is kindled in it. The implication of this statement is that they carry the lights, and that their not carrying "them" is more honourable. Do you not see that the virtue of 'Abbad ibn Bishr and Usayd ibn Hudayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, was only through a light which they did not carry? This is in this world, so how will it be in the Hereafter? From this verse is derived the carrying of a candle by the one who frees a slave (al-mu'tiq lil-shama'a). People read "wa-bi-aymanihim" as the plural of yamin (right). Sahl ibn Sa'd and Abu Haywah read "wa-bi-imanihim" with a kasra on the alif, and it is coordinated with His saying "before their hands," as if He said: sufficient before them, and existing by means of their faith.

His saying, exalted is He: "Bushrakum" means: it will be said to them, "Your good news is gardens," i.e., entry into gardens. So the governing noun was omitted and the governed noun took its place. His saying, blessed and exalted is He: "abiding therein" to the end of the verse is addressed to Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read "dhalika al-fawz al-'azim" without "huwa."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say﴾. Some grammarians (nuhat) said: "Yawm" is a substitute (badal) for the first. Others among them said: its governing element is a hidden verb whose estimate is: "remember." He said: it appears to me that its governing element is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, and the meaning of triumph becomes more majestic, as if He, exalted is He, says: the believers triumph with mercy on the Day when such and such befalls the hypocrites, because a person's rising is most splendid and majestic on the day his enemy and opponent is humiliated. The hypocrites' saying of this statement that is related occurs when their lights are extinguished, as we mentioned before. Their saying "unzurūnā" means: wait for us. From it is the verse of al-Hutay'a:

"I have waited for you as the evening drought ends, for a long time my detention and my delay have lasted."

Hamzah alone, and Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, and al-A'mash read "anzirūnā" with a hamzah at the beginning, a kasra on the zay, on the pattern of "akrama." From it is the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"O Abu Hind, do not hasten against us, and grant us respite; we will inform you with certainty."

(p-228) Its meaning is: delay us. From it is "an-nazrah ila maysarah" (respite until a time of ease), and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever grants respite to one in difficulty..." the hadith. The meaning of their saying "akhkhirūnā" is: delay your walking for us until we catch up and borrow from your light. "Iqtabasa al-rajul wa-istaqbasa" means: the man took a brand (qabas) from the light of another.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It will be said: "Turn back behind you"﴾ may be from the saying of the believers, and it may be from the saying of the angels. His saying, exalted is He: "wara'akum" (behind you): al-Mahdawi and other exegetes related that it has no place in grammatical case (i'rab), and that it is as if he said: "Turn back, turn back," and that it is like the saying of Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali to the questioner: "Behind you is wider for you." I do not know of any prohibition against its governing element being "irji'ū" (turn back). The saying to them, "Seek light," is in the sense of rebuke to them, i.e., you will not find it. Then He, mighty and majestic is He, informed that He will set up a barrier between them in this state, with a wall; the hypocrites will then struggle in darkness, and punishment from Allah, exalted is He, will seize them. It is related from Ibn Zayd that this wall is the "A'raf" mentioned in surah [al-A'raf], and al-Mahdawi related it. It was also said: it is another barrier besides that. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, Ka'b al-Ahbar, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, and Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the eastern wall of the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis. Ziyad ibn Abi Sawadah said: 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit stood upon the eastern wall of Bayt al-Maqdis, wept, and said: "From here the Prophet ﷺ informed us that he saw Jahannam."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In it is a gate called the Gate of Mercy; 'Ubadah and Ka'b named it in the interpretation of this verse. In the east of the aforementioned wall there is a valley called the Valley of Jahannam; 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, named it in the interpretation of this verse. This view about the wall is far-fetched, and Allah knows best. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the mercy is Paradise, and the punishment is Jahannam. The "sur" in the language is the enclosure of cities (p-229), and it is masculine. "Sur" is also the plural of "surah," which is a piece of a building, so that some of it is joined to another until the wall is completed; this is a collective noun that may be made masculine or feminine. This is the plural that Jarir meant in his saying:

"When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Madinah and the lofty mountains humbled themselves."

That is because Madinah never had a ... (the sense of the word here is that the walls humbled themselves), and also because describing all the buildings of Madinah as humbled is more eloquent. Whoever sees that he intended the sense of "sur" as enclosure (hijā) says: if that humbles, then other buildings are more deserving of humbling. So when "sur" in the verse may bear both meanings, it is not in the strength of the passing of winds, the chest of a spear, and other things that are purely masculine, which took the feminine from what is attached to them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Its inside contains mercy﴾: that is, the side of the believers. "Wa-zāhiruhu" (and its outside): that is, the side of the hypocrites. "Al-zahir" here means the manifest side, and from it is the phrase in books: "from the outside of the city of such-and-such."

His saying, exalted is He: "yunadūnahum" means: the hypocrites will call out to the believers: "Were we not with you in the world?" The believers will answer them: "Yes, you were with us, but you exposed yourselves to temptation, to love of the transient, and to fighting over it." Mujahid said: "You tempted yourselves with hypocrisy." "Tarabbastum" here means: with your faith, you delayed in it until you died. Qatadah said: its meaning is: you waited for us and for Muhammad ﷺ for the reversals of fortune, and you doubted the command of Allah, exalted is He. "Al-irtiyab" is doubting. "The false hopes which deceived them" are their saying: "Muhammad will perish this year; Quraysh will defeat him; the confederates will seize him," and other such hopes of theirs. Prolonged hope is a deception for everyone. It is fitting for every believer to take this verse to heart regarding himself, and regarding his procrastination in repentance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 15–17:

(p-230) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your abode is the Fire; it is your protector, and what an evil destination.﴾ ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should become humble before the remembrance of God and what has been revealed of the truth, and that they should not be like those who were given the Book before, and the term grew long for them, so their hearts hardened? Many of them are defiant.﴾ ﴿Know that God gives life to the earth after its death. We have certainly made the signs clear to you, so that you may understand.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you﴾ is a continuation of the address to the hypocrites, as Qatada and others said. Concerning the meaning of His saying, ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾, a hadith has been related: "God, exalted is He, will confront the disbeliever and say to him: 'Tell Me, if you had the equivalent of everything in the world, would you have ransomed yourself with all of that from the punishment of the Fire?' He will say: 'Yes, my Lord.' God, exalted is He, will say: 'I asked you for something easier than that while you were in the loins of your father Adam: do not associate anything with Me. But you refused except to associate.'"

The majority of reciters and people read ﴿yuʾkhadhu﴾ (is taken) with the ya' from below (yaʾ), while Abu Ja'far the reciter read ﴿tuʾkhadhu﴾ with the ta' from above (tāʾ), which is the reading of Ibn 'Amir in the transmission of Hisham from him. It is also the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'raj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿it is your protector (mawlākum)﴾. The exegetes said: its meaning is "it is more deserving of you." This is an interpretation by meaning. Rather, it is a metaphor (istiʿāra, figurative usage), because it embraces them and makes direct contact with them, so it takes on the role of their ally and stands in the place of the protector (mawlā). This is like the saying of the poet:

"…… a greeting among them is a painful blow"

(p-231) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the time not come (alam yaʾni)﴾. The verse begins a new meaning. It is related that during some of that period laughter and joking increased among a group of young Muslims, so this verse was revealed. Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: "The Companions grew weary, so the verse was revealed." The meaning of ﴿alam yaʾni﴾ is "has it not drawn near," as it is said: "the thing yaʾni (draws near) when it has arrived." From this is the saying of the poet:

"Fate has labored for him on a day that has arrived; and for every pregnant woman there is a completion."

al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read ﴿alamma yaʾni﴾. It is also related from him that he read ﴿alam yaʾin﴾. This verse is in the sense of urging and rebuke. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "The believers were reproached by this verse thirteen years after the revelation of the Qur'an began." Al-Fadl ibn Musa heard a reciter reciting this verse while al-Fadl was attempting an act of disobedience, so the verse became the cause of his repentance. al-Tha'labi related from Ibn al-Mubarak that in his youth he moved a lute to strike it, and suddenly it spoke this verse; so Ibn al-Mubarak repented, broke the lute, and success came to him.

And "al-khushu'" (humble submission) is lowering and humbling oneself. It is a state that appears in the limbs when it is in the heart; for this reason God, exalted is He, specified the heart in the mention. Shaddad ibn Aws related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The first thing that is lifted from people is khushu'." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿li-dhikri Allah (for the remembrance of God)﴾ means: for the sake of the remembrance of God and His revelation that is among them. It may also be that the meaning is: for the sake of God's reminding them and His command concerning them. 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read ﴿wa-mā nazala﴾ with a light zay. The rest, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, read ﴿wa-mā nazzala﴾ with a doubled zay, in the sense: God caused to descend (nazzala Allāhu) of the truth. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Ayyash, and it is the reading of al-Jahdari and Ibn al-Qa'qa', read ﴿wa-mā nuzzila﴾ with a kasra on the zay and doubling. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read ﴿wa-lā yakūnū﴾ with the ya' in reference to the absent party, while Hamza, as related from him by Sulaym, read ﴿wa-lā takūnū﴾ in direct address to those present.

(p-232) The indication in His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿like those who were given the Book﴾ refers to the Children of Israel contemporary with Moses, peace be upon him. This is why He said "before" (min qablu). He compared the people of one prophet's era with the people of another prophet's era. "Al-amad (the term)" has been said to mean: awaiting victory; it has been said: awaiting the Resurrection; and it has been said: the span of life. "Qasat (hardened)" means: became hard, its goodness diminished, and it ceased to respond to acts of obedience, and it found comfort in the disobedience of God, exalted is He, so they committed acts of rebellion and opposition that are transmitted of them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Know that God gives life to the earth after its death﴾. The verse addresses those believers who were urged toward humility. This is a parable and an invitation to goodness with gentleness and eloquent closeness. That is: let not your return to it and your taking it up seem distant to you, O you who have abandoned humility, for God gives life to the earth after its death. In the same way He does with hearts: He returns them to humility after their remoteness from it, and they return to it when repentance and striving come from the servant after their aversion from it, just as He gives life to the earth after it had been dead and dusty. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 18–19:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement, adornment and boasting among you, and rivalry in wealth and children, like a rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers; then it dries up, and you see it turning yellow; then it becomes debris. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verse 21–23:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Race one another to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heaven and the earth, prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾ ﴿No calamity strikes upon the earth or within yourselves except that it is in a Book before We bring it into being. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ ﴿So that you will not despair over what has eluded you, nor exult over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the forgiveness that is in the Hereafter, in this verse He urged hastening towards it and racing for it. This verse is a proof, according to all the scholars, for the recommendation of acts of obedience. Some have used it as evidence that the early part of the times of the prayers is more excellent, because it requires hastening and racing. Some of the scholars, among them Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), have mentioned in the explanation of this verse things that are by way of example. A group of scholars said: "Race one another to forgiveness from your Lord" means: be in the first row in battle. Others said, among them Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him): attend the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram) with the imam. Others said, among them 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him): be the first to enter the mosque and the last to leave it. All of this is by way of example.

He, exalted is He, mentioned the width ('ard) of the Garden, since what is customary is that the width is less than the length. A group of the people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He expressed the extent by width and did not intend that its length is greater or less. It has been reported in a hadith: "The ceiling of Paradise is the Throne," and it has been reported in a hadith: "The seven heavens within the Kursi are like a dirham in a desert, and the Kursi within the Throne is like a dirham in a desert."

His saying, exalted is He: "prepared" (u'iddat), its apparent meaning is that it is already created and prepared now, and al-Hasan stated this explicitly in the Kitab of al-Naqqash.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No calamity strikes⦆ Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: whatever event of good or evil occurs. This is according to the literal sense of the word "asaba" (strike), not according to the customary usage of "musibah" (calamity), though its customary usage is for evil. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, in substance, that he intended the customary sense of "musibah," and it was singled out for mention because it is the most important to human beings, and it is a part of the events; this indicates that all events, good and evil, are likewise. His saying, exalted is He: "in the earth" means by drought, earthquakes and other things. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor within yourselves⦆ means: by death, illnesses and other things. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except in a Book⦆ means: except that the calamity is in a Book. "Nabra'aha" means: We create it; one says: Allah "bara'a" the creation, i.e., created them. The pronoun refers to the calamity; it was also said that it refers to the earth, and it was said that it refers to the souls (anfus), as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and a group. Al-Mahdawi mentioned the permissibility of the pronoun referring to all that has been mentioned, and all of these meanings are sound, because the prior Book is eternal, before all of these. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah⦆ means: the bringing about of all things in the Book.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that you will not despair over what has eluded you⦆ means: Allah, exalted is He, did all of this and informed you of it so that it would be the cause of your submission and your lack of concern for the affairs of this world. So do not grieve over what has eluded you, and do not rejoice with the arrogant joy over what He has given you in it. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: No one does not grieve and rejoice, but whoever is struck by a calamity makes it patience, and whoever receives good makes it gratitude.

Abu 'Amr alone read "ataakum" (atākum) in the form of the past tense verb, and this is suitable with His saying, exalted is He, "faatakum." The rest of the seven read "aataakum" (ātākum) on the pattern of "a'taakum" (a'ṭākum), meaning: Allah, exalted is He, gave you (ātākumu Allāh). This is the reading of al-Hasan, al-A'raj and the people of Makkah. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read "ūtītum," which supports the reading of the majority.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful⦆ indicates that the forbidden joy is only that which leads to self-conceit and boasting. As for joy in the blessings of Allah, exalted is He, accompanied by gratitude and humility, it is a matter that no one can ward off from himself, and there is no blame in it.

This verse is a proof, according to all the scholars, for the recommendation of acts of obedience. Some have used it as evidence that the early part of the times of the prayers is more excellent, because it requires hastening and racing. Some of the scholars, among them Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), have mentioned in the explanation of this verse things that are by way of example. A group of scholars said: "Race one another to forgiveness from your Lord" means: be in the first row in battle. Others said, among them Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him): attend the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram) with the imam. Others said, among them 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him): be the first to enter the mosque and the last to leave it. All of this is by way of example.

He, exalted is He, mentioned the width ('ard) of the Garden, since what is customary is that the width is less than the length. A group of the people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He expressed the extent by width and did not intend that its length is greater or less. It has been reported in a hadith: "The ceiling of Paradise is the Throne," and it has been reported in a hadith: "The seven heavens within the Kursi are like a dirham in a desert, and the Kursi within the Throne is like a dirham in a desert."

His saying, exalted is He: "prepared" (u'iddat), its apparent meaning is that it is already created and prepared now, and al-Hasan stated this explicitly in the Kitab of al-Naqqash.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No calamity strikes⦆ Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: whatever event of good or evil occurs. This is according to the literal sense of the word "asaba" (strike), not according to the customary usage of "musibah" (calamity), though its customary usage is for evil. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, in substance, that he intended the customary sense of "musibah," and it was singled out for mention because it is the most important to human beings, and it is a part of the events; this indicates that all events, good and evil, are likewise. His saying, exalted is He: "in the earth" means by drought, earthquakes and other things. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor within yourselves⦆ means: by death, illnesses and other things. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah⦆ means: the bringing about of all things in the Book.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 24–26:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people. And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance, that people may uphold justice. And We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people, and that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Mighty.﴾ ﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham, and placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book. So among them is one who is guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

The grammarians (al-nuhat) differed over the i'rab (grammatical analysis of word endings) of "alladhina" (those who). Some of them said: they are in the place of nominative case (raf') as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) concerning them is omitted, its meaning being the threat and condemnation. Its omission is by way of vagueness, like the omission of the response in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which mountains were moved...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], the verse. Others said: they are in the nominative case as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: "They are those who are stingy." Others said: it is in the accusative case (nasb) by an implied "a'ni" (I mean) or the like. Others said: it is in the place of a descriptive attribute (sifa) of "kull" (every), because "kull," although indefinite, specifies a type of thing, and so it is permissible to describe it with a definite. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

And "yabkhaluna" (they are stingy) means: with their wealth and with their good deeds, including their faith and other things.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾ may be understood as describing them with the literal meaning of commanding by their tongues, and it may be understood as meaning that they are followed in stinginess, so they are, in that respect, as though they were commanding it.

Al-Hasan recited "bil-bukhl" with a fatha on the kha' and the ba'. The majority of reciters and the people of Iraq recited ﴿fa-inna Allaha huwa al-Ghaniyyu al-Hamid﴾ with the affirmation of "huwa" (He), and likewise in "imamihim." Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited "fa-inna Allaha al-Ghaniyya al-Hamid" without "huwa," and this is the recitation of the people of Madina, and likewise in "imamihim." No recitation is established except that it was recited before the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu 'Ali said: in the recitation in which it is established, it is fine for it to be a separating pronoun (fasl) and it is fine for it to be a subject (ibtida'), because omitting the subject is not permissible.

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is a generic noun for all the revealed books. "Al-Mizan" (the Balance): according to the interpretation of most interpreters, it means justice. Ibn Zayd and others among the interpreters said: it means the scales used among people. This is better than the first opinion, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that people may uphold justice﴾ strengthens the first opinion.

His saying, may He be exalted: "And We sent down iron" — He expressed His creating and making it by the term "sending down," as He said regarding the eight pairs of livestock. Also, since the command for things to come into being descends from the heavens, He made all of it a descent from them. Many of the majority of exegetes said: by "al-hadid" (iron) here He intends its kind, from minerals and other things. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Adam, peace be upon him, descended from the Garden with him the sindan (anvil), the kalbatan (tongs), and the miqa'a (hammer). Skilled exegetes said: He intends by it weapons. The meaning of the verse follows: Allah, may He be exalted, informed that He sent messengers, and sent down books, a just and legislated balance, and weapons, by which one fights whoever is obstinate and does not follow the guidance of Allah, so no excuse remains. In the verse, according to this interpretation, there is an urging toward fighting and an encouragement to it. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and that Allah may know who supports Him﴾ strengthens this interpretation. The meaning of His saying, may He be exalted, "that Allah may know" is: that He may know it as existing. So the change is not in Allah's knowledge, but in this occurrence that came from non-existence into existence. His saying, may He be exalted, "unseen" means: with what he heard of the unseen attributes, so he believed in them because of the evidences for them. Then He, may He be blessed and exalted, described Himself with power and might, to make clear that He has no need of support, but it is beneficial for those among people who magnify themselves by it.

Then He mentioned the mission of Noah and Abraham, peace and blessings be upon them both, honouring them by mention, and because they are among the first of the messengers, peace be upon them. Then He mentioned His blessings upon their descendants. His saying, may He be exalted, "and the Book," meaning the four books, [indicates] that among them, despite that, are those who transgressed and were obstinate. Thus, all people are likewise, and more so, which is why weapons are prescribed for fighting.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verses 27–28:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps, Our messengers, and We sent after them Jesus, son of Mary, and gave him the Gospel, and We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy, and monasticism which they invented—We did not prescribe it for them, but (they did it) seeking the pleasure of Allah—but they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy, and will appoint for you a light by which you will walk, and will forgive you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

"Qafayna" means: We brought them after the earlier ones. It is derived from "al-qafa" (the back of the neck), meaning that the second comes at the back of the first, so the first comes before the second. From this comes "al-qawafi" (rhyming final letters), which come at the ends of lines of poetry. Then Allah the Exalted mentioned Jesus, peace be upon him, for honour and distinction. Al-Hasan recited "al-Injil" with a fatha on the hamza; Abu al-Fath said: "This is a pattern (mithal) with no parallel." "Ra'fatan wa rahmatan wa rahbaniyyatan" are objects of "ja'alna" (We placed), and "ja'l" in this verse means "khalq" (creation). The phrase "ibtada'uha" (they invented it) is an attribute of "rahbaniyyatan," and it was specified as invented because compassion and mercy in the heart are not something a person acquires for himself, whereas monasticism consists of bodily acts together with something in the heart, so there is room in it for acquisition (taka assub). Qatada said: compassion and mercy are from Allah the Exalted, while monasticism is what they invented. By "compassion and mercy" is meant the love of some of them for others and their mutual affection; by "monasticism" is meant the renunciation of women and the taking of monasteries (sawami').

The Mu'tazila parse "rahbaniyyatan" as accusative by an implied verb which is explained by "ibtada'uha," and not as conjoined to "ra'fa" and "rahma." They hold that a person creates his own acts, and so they parse the verse accordingly; Abu 'Ali also parsed it this way.

It is related concerning their invention of monasticism that they split into three groups: one group fought the kings for the religion and was defeated and killed; one group remained in the cities calling to the religion and explaining it, without fighting, so the kings seized them and sawed them apart with saws, and they were killed; and one group went out to the wastelands and built monasteries and hermitages, and asked to submit (to the kings) on condition that they be left to withdraw, so they were left alone. They named themselves "al-Ruhban" (monks), and their name is derived from "al-rahab," which is fear. This is their invention. Allah the Exalted did not impose it on them, but they did it seeking the pleasure of Allah. This is the interpretation of Abu Umama and a group (of scholars). Mujahid said: the meaning is: "We prescribed it for them seeking the pleasure of Allah," so "kataba" here means "qada" (decreed). The wording may also bear the meaning: "We did not prescribe it for them except within the general category of recommended acts," because seeking the pleasure of Allah through nearness (to Him) and voluntary acts is prescribed for every community. On this possibility, the exception is "muttasil" (contiguous).

People differed concerning the pronoun in His saying, ﴿but they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾: to whom does it refer? It was said: those who invented monasticism themselves did not persist in it, nor did they fulfil its right, but rather they changed and altered it. This was said by Ibn Zayd and others, and the statement is acceptable even if there were among them those who did observe it; that is, they did not all observe it. In this interpretation is the implication that whoever begins a voluntary and supererogatory practice is bound to complete it and observe it with its proper observance. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: the pronoun refers to the kings who fought them and expelled them. Al-Dahhak and others said: the pronoun refers to the successors who came after those who invented it. The rest of the verse is clear. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "We prescribed it for them, but they invented it."

Concerning His saying, ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger﴾, people differed as to who is addressed by this. A group of the interpreters said: the address is to the People of the Book. The meaning is: O you who believe in Jesus, fear Allah and believe in Muhammad. This meaning is supported by the sound hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There are three whom Allah will give their reward twice: a man of the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me..." (the hadith). Others said: the address is to the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); it was said to them: O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger, that is: remain firm in that and persist in it. This is the meaning of the command always addressed to one who is already engaged in what he is commanded.

His saying, ﴿He will give you a double portion﴾ means: two shares, relative to what the nations before you used to be given. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Kiflayn" means "two-fold" in the language of Abyssinia. It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to one of the rabbis: "How many times was the multiplication of good deeds among you?" He said: "Three hundred and fifty." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Praise be to Allah who multiplied it for us to seven hundred." This meaning is supported by the sound hadith which states that "the Jews worked until midday for two qirats, and when the Jews and Christians argued about that, saying: 'We have done more work and are given less reward,' Allah the Exalted said: 'Have I wronged you in any of your reward?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will.'" "Al-kifl" means share and portion. "The light" here may either be a promise of the light that goes before them on the Day of Resurrection, or it may be a metaphor for the guidance by which one walks in the obedience of Allah the Exalted.

It is related concerning their invention of monasticism that they split into three groups: one group fought the kings for the religion and was defeated and killed; one group remained in the cities calling to the religion and explaining it, without fighting, so the kings seized them and sawed them apart with saws, and they were killed; and one group went out to the wastelands and built monasteries and hermitages, and asked to submit (to the kings) on condition that they be left to withdraw, so they were left alone. They named themselves "al-Ruhban" (monks), and their name is derived from "al-rahab," which is fear. This is their invention. Allah the Exalted did not impose it on them, but they did it seeking the pleasure of Allah. This is the interpretation of Abu Umama and a group (of scholars). Mujahid said: the meaning is: "We prescribed it for them seeking the pleasure of Allah," so "kataba" here means "qada" (decreed). The wording may also bear the meaning: "We did not prescribe it for them except within the general category of recommended acts," because seeking the pleasure of Allah through nearness (to Him) and voluntary acts is prescribed for every community. On this possibility, the exception is "muttasil" (contiguous).

People differed concerning the pronoun in His saying, ﴿but they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾: to whom does it refer? It was said: those who invented monasticism themselves did not persist in it, nor did they fulfil its right, but rather they changed and altered it. This was said by Ibn Zayd and others, and the statement is acceptable even if there were among them those who did observe it; that is, they did not all observe it. In this interpretation is the implication that whoever begins a voluntary and supererogatory practice is bound to complete it and observe it with its proper observance. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: the pronoun refers to the kings who fought them and expelled them. Al-Dahhak and others said: the pronoun refers to the successors who came after those who invented it. The rest of the verse is clear. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "We prescribed it for them, but they invented it."

Concerning His saying, ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger﴾, people differed as to who is addressed by this. A group of the interpreters said: the address is to the People of the Book. The meaning is: O you who believe in Jesus, fear Allah and believe in Muhammad. This meaning is supported by the sound hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There are three whom Allah will give their reward twice: a man of the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me..." (the hadith). Others said: the address is to the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); it was said to them: O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger, that is: remain firm in that and persist in it. This is the meaning of the command always addressed to one who is already engaged in what he is commanded.

His saying, ﴿He will give you a double portion﴾ means: two shares, relative to what the nations before you used to be given. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Kiflayn" means "two-fold" in the language of Abyssinia. It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to one of the rabbis: "How many times was the multiplication of good deeds among you?" He said: "Three hundred and fifty." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Praise be to Allah who multiplied it for us to seven hundred." This meaning is supported by the sound hadith which states that "the Jews worked until midday for two qirats, and when the Jews and Christians argued about that, saying: 'We have done more work and are given less reward,' Allah the Exalted said: 'Have I wronged you in any of your reward?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will.'" "Al-kifl" means share and portion. "The light" here may either be a promise of the light that goes before them on the Day of Resurrection, or it may be a metaphor for the guidance by which one walks in the obedience of Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 57, verse 29:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿That the People of the Scripture may know that they have no power over anything of the bounty of Allah, and that bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the Owner of great bounty.﴾

It is narrated that when this promise was revealed to the believers, the People of the Scripture envied them for it. The Jews magnified their religion and themselves, and claimed that they were the beloved ones of Allah and the people of His good pleasure. So this verse was revealed, informing that Allah the Exalted did this and made it known, so that the People of the Scripture would know that they are not as they claim. The "lā" in His saying, "li-allā" (lest), is superfluous, as it is in His saying: ﴿And there is a prohibition upon a city which We have destroyed, that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya' 95], according to some interpretations.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Jahdari read "li-ya'lama" (so that he may know). Ibrahim al-Taymi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, "li-kay lā ya'lama" (in order that he may not know). It is narrated from Hittan al-Ruqashi that he read "li-an ya'lama" (that he may know). Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah read "li-kay ya'lama ahl al-kitab" (in order that the People of the Scripture may know). al-Hasan, as narrated by Ibn Mujahid, read "laylan ya'lamu" with a fatha on the first lam and a sukun on the ya'. As for the fatha on the lam, it is a well-known dialectal form of the lam of genitive (lam al-jarr). The origin of this reading is "li-anna lā" (that not), the hamza was dispensed with due to the lam of genitive and so it was elided, becoming "lan lā"; the nun was assimilated into the lam because of their similarity, becoming "lil-lā"; the two similar lams came together, so one of them was changed into a ya'. al-Hasan, as narrated by Mutarrif, read "laylan" with a kasra on the first lam and a sukun on the ya', and its explanation is like the one mentioned before.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That they have no power over anything﴾ means: they do not possess the bounty of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, and it does not fall within their capacity. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read "allā yaqdiru" (that they may not have power) without the nun. The rest of the verse is clear.

The commentary on Surah [al-Hadid] is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
